extracted.intended_audience: journalism educators, media scholars, journalists and students interested in news values and press practices (particularly UK quality press)
extracted.subtask_description: An empirical and theoretical examination of how 'celebrity' and related entertainment news values have risen within the British quality press, using case studies (Elvis Presley and Michael Jackson) and quantitative measures of coverage. It is aimed at evaluating news selection, volume, placement and the implications for public interest journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrity (as a news value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Celebrity/entertainment news values have risen much higher up the hierarchy of news, guaranteeing extensive coverage if combined with other news values such as surprise and bad news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identified by Harcup and O’Neill (2001) as an added category in the taxonomy of news values. Examples include saturation coverage of Michael Jackson; can apply to both talented and self-promoting figures. Anti-patterns: colonisation of news, dumbing down, excessive focus on trivia and personal minutiae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise (untimeliness) as a news value
rubrics_metrics.description: Surprise (e.g. untimely deaths) is a traditional news value that, when combined with celebrity, increases the likelihood and volume of coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in analysis to explain heightened coverage of sudden celebrity deaths (Michael Jackson). Cited as one of Harcup & O'Neill's and Galtung & Ruge's relevant news values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad news as a news value
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad news (tragic or scandalous events) increases newsworthiness and combines with celebrity to drive intensive coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: tragic deaths, scandals (e.g. later revelations about Jimmy Savile). Works as an amplifier of celebrity news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entertainment as a news value
rubrics_metrics.description: Entertainment content and entertainment-driven stories function as a news value that can justify inclusion despite limited 'serious' informational content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often indistinguishable from celebrity coverage; contributes to the blurring of news and entertainment formats. May be legitimate but problematic when it displaces public-interest reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elite people / 'Power elite' vs celebrity distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: "Elite people" (power elite) was found by Harcup & O'Neill to be too broad, and the UK press treats many 'elite' items as celebrities (soap stars, sports stars, film stars, royalty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides evaluators to distinguish traditional power-elite newsworthiness (political, economic influence) from celebrity fame; cautions against conflating celebrity prominence with elite public-interest relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest / Watchdog function
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism's core role as watchdog—holding power to account and informing the public—is a fundamental criterion against which celebrity journalism should be judged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If reporting fails to inform, it 'ceases to be journalism' (Harcup). Celebrity stories should be evaluated on whether they contribute to public interest, not solely on entertainment value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility and authority of quality press
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality newspapers' unique selling point is perceived credibility and authority; this should guide editorial choices, especially in the digital era.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and journalists are urged to protect authoritative coverage as a differentiator from tabloids; over-emphasis on celebrity can weaken claims to credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volume / saturation of coverage (proportion of news)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sheer volume and saturation of celebrity coverage—often measured as a percentage of news pages—determines whether celebrity is displacing other news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper argues there is an 'unwritten rule' that such stories receive saturation coverage. Empirical measure used: percentage of domestic news column inches devoted to a celebrity. Anti-pattern: near-half of domestic news pages devoted to one celebrity (e.g. Guardian and Times on day of Jackson death).

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement: domestic news pages vs overseas/features/supplements
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a story appears (domestic news pages, overseas pages, features or supplements) affects its prominence and whether it displaces other hard news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study distinguishes coverage on domestic news pages from overseas or feature sections; some stories (Presley) were treated as overseas and given less domestic prominence, unlike Jackson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal window / timeliness (vortextuality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intensity and timing of coverage (e.g. the concentrated 'vortextuality' or short-lived intense focus on an event) is a criterion for assessing media behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study uses a three-day window following deaths to compare peaks; Whannel's 'vortextuality' explains rapid, self-referential media focus. Temporal spread (weeks/months) also relevant for long-tail coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative measurement: column inches methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure column inches of print text (photos excluded) on news pages; calculate the number devoted to the celebrity and express as a percentage of total news coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific protocol used in the case study: exclude photos, record total column inches on news pages, compute celebrity column inches as percent of domestic news; note and separately record coverage appearing in supplements/features but exclude them from the percentage if not on news pages; when coverage appears on overseas pages express as percent of domestic news and of all news (bracketed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Case selection/comparability criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose comparable celebrities for longitudinal comparison: subjects should have achieved celebrity by talent (preferably in pop music), similar fame levels, died prematurely, and fit similar narrative arcs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale used for selecting Elvis Presley and Michael Jackson: comparable global pop-star status, premature deaths, and similar fame trajectories enabling cross-decade comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article-counting via lead-paragraph searches
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantify media attention by counting articles that mention the celebrity in the lead/first paragraph (e.g. Newsbank searches showing 3162 lead mentions of Jackson in period).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to assess breadth of ongoing coverage beyond the immediate news pages and to compare prominence with political figures (e.g. Jackson vs Home Secretary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on PR and 'cultural intermediaries'
rubrics_metrics.description: The symbiotic relationship with PR industry (agents, publicists, promoters, etc.) increases celebrity coverage and can result in manipulated or puff pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies an evaluative criterion: stories sourced from PR and publicity are more likely to be uncritical, speculative, or lazy; this is an anti-pattern for quality journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intertextuality / media bandwagon / pack mentality
rubrics_metrics.description: Media outlets often follow rivals' agendas, feeding off each other and creating rapid, self-preferential amplification of celebrity stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This dynamic (pack mentality, bandwagon effects) is a criterion for diagnosing why celebrity items dominate; evaluators should note cross-media echoing and the speed amplification from digital/social media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy, truthfulness and avoidance of speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Truthful and accurate information is a core standard; omission of truthful material or propagation of unsubstantiated gossip undermines claims to be a newspaper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article stresses that if truthful and accurate information is omitted, publications lose legitimacy. Anti-patterns include rumours, speculation and unverified gossip common in celebrity reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics: privacy, legality and invasive reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethical limits around privacy and illegal practices (e.g. voicemail hacking) are critical evaluative criteria for journalistic practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights real harms from invasive reporting practices; evaluators should weigh public interest against invasions of privacy and unlawful newsgathering methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between informing and entertaining
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism must both inform and entertain; the balance is a criterion—entertainment should not replace informative, accountability-focused reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harcup quote: if stories are 'too dull' nobody will engage, but entertainment should not equate to trivial celebrity minutiae that displace substantive news. Educators should teach discerning this difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical continuity/change in news values
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether contemporary news values represent a shift from past taxonomies (e.g. Galtung & Ruge 1965) to newer ones including Celebrity (Harcup & O'Neill 2001).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical comparison to determine whether celebrity's ascendancy is new or part of a longer continuity; this informs judgments about 'dumbing down' vs stylistic evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial design and pagination considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in pagination, layout, design and the presence of more pages/photos affect how coverage volume should be interpreted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing across decades, account for vastly increased pagination and visual/feature space; use proportional measures (percentages) to control for these differences.
